title: continuous-batching-scheduler-tuning-experiments-15
content:
Summary:

These are the notes and experiment logs from the continuous-batching scheduler tuning work (round 15). Goal: find a robust default config that improves throughput without regressing 95/99th tail latency for our medium-length chat workload (avg seq_len ~160 tokens). Secondary goals: reduce unfair head-of-line blocking between clients, and ensure graceful degradation under bursty traffic.

Context / motivation:
- We've been seeing good aggregate throughput gains with aggressive batching, but some tenants report high p99 spikes during mixed-priority workloads.
- Previous rounds (1-14) covered micro-optimizations and early heuristics; this round focuses on scheduler-level knobs: max_batch_size, batch_timeout_ms, fairness_weight, age-based priority, and per-model backpressure limits.
- Environment: staging cluster (4x A100-40GB), serving-runtime branch: scheduler-experiments/v15. Workload generator mimics product chat traffic (Poisson arrival, mean QPS=75, 20% short requests (<=32 tokens), 70% medium (64-256), 10% long (>=512)).

Profiling & telemetry used:
- Flame traces collected with pprof instrumentation inside scheduler and worker (span-level).
- nvprof/Nsight telemetry for kernel utilization and GPU occupancy on sample runs.
- eBPF-based syscall traces to rule out blocking in userland.
- Per-request traces via TraceID -> saved for 1000 slowest traces per run.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency (request end-to-end), batching wait time (time spent queued waiting for batch), GPU active token throughput (tokens/s), batch formation distribution (histogram of batch sizes), fairness metrics (variance of latencies across client-id groups).

Experiment matrix (high level):
1) Baseline (v14 defaults): max_batch_size=64, batch_timeout_ms=8, fairness_weight=0.0 (strict throughput-first), age_boost=false
2) Aggressive batching: max_batch_size=128, batch_timeout_ms=12, fairness_weight=0.0
3) Low timeout: max_batch_size=64, batch_timeout_ms=2, fairness_weight=0.0
4) Fairness-first: max_batch_size=64, batch_timeout_ms=8, fairness_weight=0.7, age_boost=true
5) Hybrid: max_batch_size=96, batch_timeout_ms=6, fairness_weight=0.4, age_boost=true
6) Per-model caps: same as hybrid but with per-model concurrent batch cap=4 to avoid hogging by large-model jobs
7) Tail-safe: conservative settings for tail (max_batch_size=48, batch_timeout_ms=4) with fairness_weight=0.5

Key raw observations (median of 5 runs each):
- Baseline: throughput ~18k tokens/s, p50=42ms, p95=115ms, p99=238ms. Batch size median=54, 90th percentile batch size=64. Batch wait time median=3.6ms, p95=9.4ms. GPU occupancy ~78%.
- Aggressive batching: throughput +22% vs baseline (~22k tokens/s), p50 improved to 36ms, p95 slightly worse 130ms, p99 regressed to 310ms. Batch size median=96, p95=128, batch wait time median=7.2ms. Observed occasional 200-400ms queuing spikes for single-tenant long sequences. GPU occupancy ~88% (higher).
- Low timeout: throughput -7% (~16.7k tokens/s), p50=48ms, p95=105ms, p99=215ms. Batch sizes smaller (median=40). Reduced extreme p99 spikes (fewer outliers). GPU occupancy ~70%.
- Fairness-first: throughput -10% (~16.2k tokens/s), p50=50ms, p95=98ms, p99=180ms. Variance of latencies across client groups reduced by ~45%. Batch sizes median=50, p95=66. Age-boost prevented starvation of small clients.
- Hybrid: throughput -1% (~17.8k tokens/s), p50=44ms, p95=99ms, p99=192ms. Best balance: throughput close to baseline but much better p99 than aggressive. Batch sizes median=68, p95=96.
- Per-model caps: throughput -3% vs hybrid (~17.3k tokens/s), p99 similar to hybrid, but observed better tail isolation when a large-model tenant injected bursts.
- Tail-safe: throughput -12% (~15.8k tokens/s), p99=168ms, very stable tails, but overall cost per token increases due to lower utilization.

Detailed trace analysis:
- Aggressive runs: many of the p99 traces show a long batching wait (120-280ms) waiting for similar-length requests to arrive and form a big batch. After batch formed, GPU execution time per token is slightly lower (due to kernel efficiency), but the end-to-end latency for those requests is dominated by queueing.
- Low timeout runs: queueing time reduced, but more small batches increased GPU kernel launch overheads and slightly reduced throughput.
- Fairness-first: age_boost counteracted head-of-line blocking. We saw requests from low-QPS clients get scheduled earlier, reducing variance. Some throughput loss is from breaking up hot batches.

GPU profiling notes:
- Nsight shows better SM utilization for larger batches but more kernel queueing; kernel latency per token decreases ~7% when batch size doubles from 48->96 for this model.
- Memory copy and KV cache point-in-time usage is stable; observed no memcpy stalls.
- On A100 40GB runs, peak GPU memory used ~28GB; no OOM.

Fairness metric definition used here (for these experiments):
- fairness_score = 1 - (stddev(latency_per_client_group) / mean(latency_per_client_group)). Used to compare fairness knobs across runs.

Conclusions / recommended default for staging->prod trial:
- Hybrid config (max_batch_size=96, batch_timeout_ms=6, fairness_weight=0.4, age_boost=true) is the best single-point tradeoff for mixed workloads: it preserves ~98-101% of baseline throughput while improving p99 by ~20% relative to the aggressive setting and reducing latency variance across tenants.
- Add per-model concurrent batch cap (default 4) to protect small-model tenants from long-sequence hogs. This cap can be raised for dedicated customers with guaranteed capacity.
- Expose a tail-safe profile (conservative) for customers that require strict p99 SLAs; document cost tradeoff.
- Consider adaptive timeout: increase batch_timeout_ms when the scheduler detects high sequence-length homogeneity and low fairness risk; decrease timeout during heterogeneous or multi-tenant load.

Next experiments (action items):
- Implement adaptive-timeout prototype (A/B with hybrid) and run under bursty mixed workloads.
- Add synthetic tenant burst tests to quantify per-model cap effectiveness at scale (10 tenants, 3 heavy, 7 light).
- Drive end-to-end canary in prod on a small set of customers (opt-in) with hybrid defaults + telemetry hooks for p99 alerts.
- Work with console team to add a per-tenant "batching profile" toggle and visualization of batch formation distribution.

Open questions / risks:
- Interaction with token caching: when prefix KV cache hits are high, batching same-prefix requests may be cheaper; need to ensure cache warmness heuristics are compatible with batching heuristics.
- Long tail behavior on multi-region routing: cross-region fallback creates heterogeneity in queueing; need to test scheduler with cross-region traces.
- Fairness-weight calibration: 0.4 worked well on our simulated mixes; we need to validate across customer traffic shapes.

Appendix: quick run checklist
- Repro steps: checkout scheduler-experiments/v15, deploy to staging with 4xA100 config used for tests, run workload-generator/{mixed-chat,burst-tenants} for 10 minutes per config, collect traces (pprof) and nvprof summary.
- Key dashboards: /dashboards/serving/runtime/batching (new), tail-traces (saves bad traces), cpu/gpu-kernel-latency.
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/431 (scheduler knobs + telemetry hooks)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc; numbers are medians from our runs and should be considered guidance.
- Please comment if you see missing telemetry (e.g., per-tenant GPU allocation breakdown) that would help tighten recommendations.

-- Priya
